entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: shared aligner, wider stem
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c3, but the per-cell 1x1 stem widens from 64 to 128 hidden units. Stacking correctly means comparing, cell by cell, the build height with each aligned target and missing layer, which is a multiplicative layer-selection job. r3c3 gets layer 0 right but fails on upper layers. The cost is about 14% more compute, so about 127k steps. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.174 or the agent still places few bricks above layer 0.
entries.last_analysis: The key problem is aligning the shifted target with the build. A full-grid circular kernel shared by all channels (r3c3, 0.174, both seeds 0.14 and 0.21) clearly beats per-channel kernels (about 0.077), the per-axis kernels (0.039) and a non-equivariant Linear (0). The main failure is collapsing to DONE early, which leaves dev success at 0. It hit 2 epochs, lr 0.002 and gamma 0.99, all with weaker or same-network aligners. Collapse looks like a race: the agent must learn rewarding placements before DONE's 0 reward wins. A faster-learning aligner wins that race. r3c3 gets layer 0 almost right but stops early, misses upper layers and does not handle overhangs. For the final round all three candidates keep the shared aligner and change one thing each: more samples (2 epochs), more per-cell capacity for comparing layers, and better credit for the exact-build bonus (longer rollouts, lambda 0.95).

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: best + lr 0.002
entries.hypothesis: Keep r2c2's network and 1 PPO epoch, and raise lr from 0.001 to 0.002. The learning rate decays linearly to 0, and the r2c2 curve levels off after 75% of training. A larger step size should reach the plateau sooner and go further while the learning rate is still useful. Expect a mean above 0.94. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.92, or if the two seeds diverge, which would mean training became unstable.
entries.last_analysis: The observed target is the real design rolled by X/2 columns. Adding a rolled copy of the observation fixed this (0.59 versus 0.19 for the learned full-row stem). After that, getting more fresh samples mattered most: 1 PPO epoch beat 2 and 4, at 0.935. Raising lr to 0.002 gave the best result so far, 0.953, with seeds 0.945 and 0.961. Outcomes switch between modes. Several runs got stuck in a 'build layer 0 then DONE' trap (IoU 0.714, about 0.08 success): both circular-stem runs, both r3c2 seeds and one r3c3 seed. r3c3's other seed fell into the 'DONE at once' trap. So the third conv and the context-bias results may be partly seed bad luck, but adding them was risky. In this last round I keep r3c1's network, which seems stable, and change one recipe setting per candidate. Gaps under about 0.02 should be treated as noise.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, so there is no gradient to follow and no noise estimate beyond "all zero". The trials covered recipe changes (1 or 2 epochs, gamma 0.95 to 0.995), per-layer heads, a dense action head, a layout-free MLP and action-query attention. Failing every way suggests either that exact builds are out of reach at this budget, or that the world differs from its description in a way none of these designs exploited. The MLP's failure argues against a simple action-layout mismatch alone. The baseline's receptive field is shallow (two 3x3 convs) and its updates are few and large. For this last round I'm placing three different bets: (1) the baseline with many small, sharp, short-horizon updates; (2) a deeper fully convolutional ResNet whose head is a learned conv over each footprint window; (3) a small transformer that sees the whole grid, for ordering that depends on distant cells.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: I can't see any scores, so these choices rest on priors, not evidence. Every trial so far trained without errors, including 1 epoch at 405k steps (r2c1), so time limits aren't a risk at these sizes. My priors: (1) with a fresh design every episode and a dense reward, more samples per FLOP (fewer PPO epochs) probably helps; (2) gamma 0.99 should carry the +1 exact-build bonus back to early placements; (3) the global broadcast costs almost nothing and gives each placement score the overall build state; (4) attention or depth could help with ordering, at a cost in samples. This is the last round, so I'm aiming for the strongest combinations rather than clean single-variable tests. All three candidates use 1 PPO epoch with gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95. They differ only in the network's context range: local (the base network plus the broadcast), global attention, or a deeper conv trunk with a stem skip.

entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: r3c1 + 3 epochs (more samples)
entries.hypothesis: r3c1's network and 128 worlds, with 3 PPO epochs instead of 4. The budget then gives about 1.3x more samples (about 159k steps) and about 78 updates instead of 58. r3c1's training success leveled off near 0.85 late in training, so more fresh data may help more than a fourth pass over old data. Refuted if dev success falls below 0.83.
entries.last_analysis: Two things matter most. First, the policy head must pool over the flipped features (mirror-concat), so it scores the cells where a brick will really land. Second, the DONE head should see the detached placement logits. Halving n_envs to 128 (r3c1) lifted dev success from 0.68 to 0.88, with both seeds close together. r2c3 and r3c1 both took 3,712 gradient steps with 128-sample minibatches. So the gain came from collecting data with a more recent policy, not from more optimisation. The training curve for r3c1 levels off at about 0.85 from 75% of training onward. A footprint-shaped convolution in the head (r3c2) did worse. Gamma 0.99 (r3c3) also did worse. 2 epochs (r2c2) was mixed and noisy. For the last round, all three candidates keep the r3c1 network and push further along the axis that worked. One halves n_envs again to 64. One uses 3 epochs, which buys more samples and updates. One combines both changes to give the best chance at the final result.

entries.label: r3c2
entries.name: flip, 1 epoch, 64 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Change: ppo_epochs 1 as in the first candidate, plus n_minibatches 64 (64 samples per minibatch). This keeps about 426k steps and doubles the gradient steps per sample. Why: one epoch with 32 minibatches gives slightly fewer optimiser steps than r2c1, so the agent might gain samples but lose fitting. Refuted if this scores below the 1-epoch, 32-minibatch candidate by more than the seed noise of about 6 points, or below 0.90.
entries.last_analysis: Two changes account for almost all of the progress. The x-flip before the head fixed the mirrored action mapping (0 to 0.75). Fewer PPO epochs, which buys more samples, raised success further: 3 epochs gave 0.79, 2 gave 0.90, 1 gave 0.92, and 1 epoch with 64 minibatches gave 0.96 (best, seeds 0.97 and 0.95). Several ideas did not help: learned axis mixing (0.04), global context added to the head (0.78), the dilated conv (0.72) and gamma 0.99 (0.82, within noise of its comparison). Seed noise is about 2 to 6 points. r3c2's training success stops rising at about 0.90 by 75% of training with the entropy coefficient at 0.03. That suggests more learning per sample (higher learning rate) or less exploration noise. The remaining errors are a few cells placed outside the target, which suggests the head sometimes misjudges landing layers. Raw per-column layer features passed straight to the head may fix that.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success was also 0 in every run. This held across three architecture families (the start net, the layer-conditioned head and the layer-sliced net) and across recipes (more updates, 1 or 2 epochs, 3x the samples, small output initialisation). Seed noise alone cannot explain this. A dense shaped reward with roughly 400k samples should give at least occasional exact builds, so something basic is probably broken. The task warns that the world may not match its description. One likely mismatch is that the action indexing is not aligned with the observation grid (transposed, flipped, or a different anchor). If so, every convolutional footprint head we tried puts each action's logit at the wrong cells, and a local convolution cannot learn that non-local shift. This last round tests that idea with heads that can learn any mapping from cells to actions.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: I can't see any scores, so I'm choosing on design reasoning, not on evidence. All 9 trials trained without errors. Three lines have been tried: recipes that give more samples (2 epochs, then 1 epoch with lr 0.002, up to about 405k steps), a per-layer landing head that matches the drop rule, and wider context (a deeper trunk with a global broadcast, or cell self-attention). Each run uses 2 seeds, and the final pick is the best 2-seed score, so in this last round I'll combine the parts that are most likely to be strong rather than repeat a trial. I'll add the 1-epoch, data-rich recipe to the per-layer head, which has been tried with 4 and 2 epochs but not 1. I'll put the per-layer head on the attention trunk, so the head handles landing and attention handles ordering. I'll run the attention trunk with the 1-epoch recipe. All three stay under about 1.5x compute and use only 2D operations, so they should finish well inside the time limit.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: circular stem, long horizon
entries.hypothesis: Same as r1c2 but with gamma 0.99 and gae_lambda 0.95. With gamma 0.95, the +1 exact-build bonus is discounted to about 0.6 by the time it reaches early placements. That weakens credit for build order (fill under overhangs before covering them) and for finishing instead of stopping early. A longer horizon should raise exact builds and placements per episode. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.43, or if episodes still end early.
entries.last_analysis: Lining up the rolled target with the build is what unlocks learning. The starting network and every trial without circular row mixing collapsed to choosing DONE at once. Seed 0 is the bottleneck. It scored exactly 0.0781 in four different trials, so it reliably settles into a policy that fills layer 0 only and then stops. That suggests stacking is hard to perceive, because the conjunction 'build filled at z-1 here and target missing at z four columns away' must be learned inside one wide row conv. The recipe changes (more samples, a longer horizon, more entropy, small-gain initialisation) moved the mean by no more than seed noise. r1c1, with the default 4 epochs, had the most balanced seeds (0.31 / 0.49). The full-row and full-column trunk failed (seed 0 chose DONE immediately). The per-layer stem helped seed 0 only with entropy 0.04, and seed 1 fell at the same time. Final round: test a factorised alignment layer under two recipes, plus r1c1 with a long horizon.

entries.label: r3c3
entries.name: half-roll, 4x updates, lr 2e-3
entries.hypothesis: Same as r2c1, but lr goes from 0.001 to 0.002. With only about 120 updates and training success still rising at the end, a bigger step size should get further within the budget. PPO clipping and gradient clipping should limit instability. Refuted if dev success falls below about 0.86, or one seed collapses, which would mean the bottleneck is update count rather than step size.
entries.last_analysis: The observed target is shifted by X//2 columns. Adding a half-rolled copy of the observation fixed this: the score went from 0 to 0.59. After that, the recipe mattered most. Refreshing data more often at the same number of gradient steps (128→64 envs, 128 samples per minibatch) raised dev success from 0.82 to 0.885, and lr 2e-3 raised it to 0.913 (best; both seeds about 0.90 or higher). Going further failed. Rollout_len 8 collapsed (0.076), probably from heavy bootstrapping and tiny advantage batches. Two epochs with 128 envs lost one seed (0.90 vs 0.15). The global broadcast gave no clear gain (0.874 vs 0.885). At the end of training, training success (0.90) roughly equals dev success, so the limit is how fast the agent learns, not generalisation or capacity. A bigger network would cost samples and updates. For this last round I keep the best architecture and change one optimisation setting per candidate: a higher lr, 3 PPO epochs (about 30% more fresh samples and updates), and a lower entropy bonus so the greedy policy sharpens sooner.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis:
All nine trials scored 0 on both seeds, and none had any exact build during training. Recipe changes (1 or 2 epochs, smaller batches, higher entropy, longer horizon) did not change this. Neither did head rearrangements meant to fix a possible action-layout mismatch, a transformer trunk, or a column MLP. So the evidence cannot rank anything yet, and the next step is a structural guess.

Two bottlenecks are plausible. First, DONE: an exact build only counts if the agent chooses DONE at exactly the right step. In a flat softmax over about 257 actions, DONE starts near 0.4% and gets crowded out as placement logits sharpen, so the +1 bonus may never be found. Second, landing-layer perception: a good placement needs 'the highest build cell under the footprint is z, and the target is missing at layer z in every footprint cell'. These are per-layer comparisons that 2D trunks blur.

This round therefore tests a separate stop/continue head (on the baseline and on a new per-layer network) and the per-layer network on its own.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so the choice rests on task structure. The footprint-window head (r1c2/r2c2/r3c1) scores each placement from the exact covered cells, which looks like the most fitting design. Recipes with fewer epochs trade data reuse for more fresh designs (307k steps with 1 epoch) and stay inside the time limit. A brick lands on the highest filled cell under its footprint, which needs a max over the covered cells. A linear window conv plus one ReLU computes this poorly, while max/min pooling gives it directly. So a head combining the window conv with pooling is the most promising refinement. For this last round I give the combined head two recipes (2 epochs, and 1 epoch with the legal-action mask as input). The third candidate keeps r3c1's network and tests a longer horizon with lower entropy for sharper greedy play.

entries.label: r1c3
entries.name: mirror flip + global context
entries.hypothesis: Mirror flip plus the recipe with more updates, and two additions: a third residual conv with dilation 2, and a global context vector (mean and max of the features) broadcast to every cell. Placement order depends on non-local facts, such as whether supports elsewhere are already built and how much of the target is still missing. This costs about 1.3× the starting compute. Refuted if it scores below the mirror-flip run with the same recipe.
entries.last_analysis: Flipping the features left-right is the change that matters: without it the agent always learns to stop at DONE, and with it dev success goes from 0 to 0.64–0.89. The best result is r1c3 (flip plus global context, 0.886), and both its seeds score well. None of the later changes beat it. Gamma 0.99 scored 0.846, which is within noise. Self-attention scored 0.78 and cut the sample budget. The per-layer encoder scored 0.42. The slim network with more samples scored 0.870, which ties r1c3, so width barely matters. Two results point at entropy and seed stability. Lowering ent_coef to 0.003 made both seeds worse (0.74), which suggests more exploration might help. Halving n_envs led to a full collapse to DONE on one seed. Dev IoU is about 0.98 and roughly 0.3–0.5 cells per episode land outside the target, so the remaining errors are a few wrong placements per design. For this last round I make three single changes to r1c3: a higher entropy bonus, fewer PPO epochs to get more samples, and a uniform starting policy.

entries.label: r2c3
entries.name: best + long-horizon credit
entries.hypothesis: Same as r1c2 but with gamma 0.99 and gae_lambda 0.95. Ordering mistakes, such as filling a cell under an overhang too early, are made early but only cost the +1 exact-build bonus at DONE about 10 steps later. With gamma 0.95 and lambda 0.9 that signal is heavily discounted and biased. Longer credit should teach the network to avoid placements that block the design. Refuted if dev success is no higher than 0.887 or drops.
entries.last_analysis: The x-mirror remap is what made the task learnable (0 → 0.75). The best results are r2c3 (0.888, seeds 0.889 and 0.887) and r1c2 (0.887). Both use 128 envs and ent_coef 0.02, and r2c3 also uses gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95. Changes that gave more updates or more samples (2 or 3 epochs, 64 envs) raised the best single seed to 0.91, but often made one seed collapse to about 0.45. So the 2-seed mean is limited by instability, not by capacity. Spending compute on the network (a third conv, a per-layer head, a footprint conv) cut samples and scored lower. Dev IoU is about 0.985, so the remaining errors are a few wrong or out-of-order bricks. In this last round I keep the r2c3 network and try to stabilise training: more but smaller updates with a lower learning rate, longer rollouts so returns are cut off less often, and per-pixel LayerNorm in the trunk.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Nine trials, all at 0 on both seeds and 0 train success: recipe changes (2 or 1 epochs, 59 to 208 updates), heads (footprint pooling, per-layer logsumexp, 3x3 conv, transformer, dense mixer, dihedral) and trunks all failed. A design of 6 bricks should sometimes be built by chance during training, and that never happened. This suggests a systematic mismatch, not slow learning. The world 'may not behave as described', and the likeliest hidden difference is the action layout. Spatial heads cannot learn a cell-major index (cell*n_types + type) or an x-major index (x*Y + y), and the dense head learns too slowly. Flips alone (dihedral) were already ruled out. In this last round, every candidate emits placement logits under four flatten layouts at once (type/cell-major × y/x-major) and sums them, so training can switch off the wrong ones. Each also feeds the mask in matching layouts.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only reason from the design of the trials. All 9 trials trained without errors. Two seeds per trial are noisy, so the last round should spread its bets over likely-strong configurations rather than test outlying ideas. Based on the budget formula, I expect sample count and update count to matter most at this small budget. The 2-epoch recipe with 2048 steps per update (r2c1, r3c1) gives about 230k samples and about 110 updates while keeping the network cheap. The stem skip (r3c1) gives the placement head the exact per-column features, which is a reasonable prior for learning landing heights. All three proposals build on r3c1 and make one change each: a cheap global context added to every cell before the head; learned convolutions over each brick's footprint in the head; and a higher gamma so the exact-build bonus reaches early placements.

entries.label: r2c1
entries.name: r1c2 with ppo_epochs 2
entries.hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r1c2, but ppo_epochs drops from 4 to 2. The compute budget then allows about 1.86x as many environment steps (about 242k, 118 updates), with a similar total number of gradient steps. r1c2's training curve was still climbing, so fresher and more varied designs should help it generalise. Refuted if dev success is at or below r1c2's 0.865 within noise (about 0.03).
entries.last_analysis: The circular full-width row conv works because it lets each column see the target shifted by 4. It took the score from 0 to 0.60, then to 0.87 with 64 updates and entropy 0.02, then to 0.92 with ppo_epochs 2 (r2c1). Without alignment, attention (r1c3) collapsed to DONE. The main risk is that the policy learns to choose DONE immediately. Early random placements earn negative reward and DONE earns 0, so any change that slows early learning or makes placement returns more negative tips it over: ppo_epochs 1 collapsed (1 seed fully, the other scored 0.15), as did gamma 0.99 and the bigger net with 1 epoch. Dev failures are now rare (IoU 0.986, about 0.44 extra cells per episode), so the remaining gains must come from order and support reasoning. For this last round I keep r2c1's base and make small changes that should not raise the collapse risk: more entropy, more gradient steps at the same data, and one more residual layer at 2 epochs.

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: r2c1 + 2 PPO epochs
entries.hypothesis: Same network as r2c1, with ppo_epochs 2 instead of 4. Under the budget formula this gives about 1.86x more environment steps (about 190k), with a similar total number of gradient steps. r2c1's curve was still climbing steeply, so fresh designs should help more than reusing old samples. Refuted if the mean is below about 0.42, or if any seed collapses to DONE.
entries.last_analysis: The observed target is shifted cyclically by X/2 along x, so it does not line up with the build. Adding a copy of the target rolled back by X/2 (r2c1, 0.48) was the breakthrough. Without it, runs collapse to DONE. The rest of the gain came from more samples per FLOP. With 2 PPO epochs, r3c1 reached 0.76 (0.82 and 0.69). With 1 epoch and 64-sample minibatches, r3c3 averaged 0.50, but its seeds diverged: 0.91 and 0.08. One epoch can reach a higher score but is unstable. Its seed-0 training success reached 0.89 and was still rising. Lower lr with more entropy (r2c2) slowed learning. Higher gamma (r3c2) hurt and made the agent stop early. In this last round I try to make the high-sample regime stable. Two levers: larger minibatches (less gradient noise) and a zero-initialised policy output (uniform start, less early drift toward DONE). One candidate isolates zero-init on the 2-epoch best.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis:
After 9 trials, every run scored exactly 0: dev success and training success, on both seeds. The trials covered footprint-pooling heads, per-layer gated heads, footprint-kernel convs, generic deep convs and a transformer, with recipes from 4 epochs down to 1 epoch at about 426k steps and gamma up to 0.99. Because the generic architectures also failed, a wrong guess about channels or the anchor convention is probably not the main cause.

My leading suspicion is that the policy collapses early onto DONE. At the start most placements are wrong and earn negative reward, while DONE ends the episode at 0, so the policy may learn to stop before it ever finds exact builds. The results don't show this directly; it is a hypothesis.

For the final round I apply the same fix to three different architectures (generic residual conv, footprint-kernel conv, baseline). Each adds the legality mask as learned input channels and a constant -2 offset on the DONE logit. Each uses 1 PPO epoch for the most samples, with gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95. If all three still score 0, collapse onto DONE was not the bottleneck.

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: Column-skip + dilated context conv
entries.hypothesis: Adds a third residual 3x3 conv with dilation 2 to r1c2. The receptive field grows from 5x5 to about 9x9, which covers the whole 8x8 grid. The agent can then see distant missing cells and the supports an overhang needs, which governs the safe build order, and DONE and value get better features. Cost is about r=1.35. Refuted if it scores no better than r1c2. That would mean decisions are local and the samples it costs are wasted.
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so these choices come from reasoning, not measured results. All earlier trials trained without errors. The column-skip head is the most plausible network gain because it costs almost nothing (r≈1.08). The costlier options (attention, per-layer head, wider head) leave fewer training samples. Exact-build success depends on the +1 bonus at episode end, which gamma 0.95 heavily discounts, so gamma 0.99 with lambda 0.95 is the recipe change most likely to help. Fewer PPO epochs (2) give about 1.8x more fresh designs, which should help generalisation. In this last round I combine these plausible gains: (A) column-skip with long horizon and the sample-heavy recipe; (B) dilated full-grid context with long horizon; (C) a new idea, the legality mask reshaped to per-type maps and fed in as learned input, which hints at landing height near the top of the stack, with long horizon.

entries.label: r2c1
entries.name: Reflection head, 2 PPO epochs
entries.hypothesis: Same as r1c1, but with ppo_epochs set to 2. Under the fixed budget this nearly doubles environment samples (about 217k versus 119k). Training success was still climbing steeply at the end, so the run is short of samples. Refuted if dev success is not above r1c1's 0.726 by more than seed noise (about 0.06), or if it drops because each sample is reused less.
entries.last_analysis: Mirroring the features is the key fix. Models with mirrored features score 0.63–0.87, while the starting network and the learned remapping score 0.00–0.04. Under fixed compute, more fresh samples help: going from 4 to 2 PPO epochs raised dev success from 0.726 to 0.871 (r2c1). One epoch collapsed to choosing DONE immediately. Combining 2 epochs with smaller batches was unstable, with one seed at 0.27 (r3c1). With smaller batches, gamma 0.99 brought that combination back to 0.838 with stable seeds (r3c3). Remaining failures are near misses (IoU about 0.98, about 0.5 extra cells per episode), so longer-horizon credit may help. The action-frame trunk (r2c3) was cheaper and slightly better than concatenation at 4 epochs (within noise) but was never tried with the better recipe. Since this is the last round, I prefer changes to the best that should be stable across seeds.

entries.label: r4c3
entries.name: flip, half batches, ent 0.01
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c1 but ent_coef 0.01. The higher entropy was added to stop an early collapse onto DONE, but with n_envs 128 the agent already learns quickly (0.29 training success at 25%). A lower entropy bonus should let the policy sharpen, so greedy and training behaviour match more closely and exact builds are more reliable. Refuted if dev success falls below about 0.92 or a seed collapses to DONE.
entries.last_analysis: Rounds 1–3 found one big fix: actions are mirrored along x relative to the observation, and flipping the features before the footprint head fixes it (0 → 0.75). Every gain after that came from the recipe. Cutting ppo_epochs from 4 to 2 gave 0.93; 1 epoch gave 0.92. Halving n_envs to 128 so there are twice as many updates gave the best score, 0.949 (r3c1), and the fastest early learning (0.29 training success at 25% of training, against 0.00 before). Changes that did not help or made things worse: lr 2e-3 (0.933, within noise), gamma 0.99 (0.87), a deeper trunk (0.82), moving compute into the head (0.86) and a learned axis remap (0). Seed spread is about 2–5 points. The evidence says this budget is limited by how many updates training gets, not by the network's capacity. For this last round I keep r3c1's network and push the update-frequency lever further: smaller batches, 1 epoch with more samples, and lower entropy now that early learning is fast.

entries.label: r4c3
entries.name: Deeper trunk with whole-board context
entries.hypothesis: New idea on top of r3c1: a third residual block, plus a pooled summary of the whole board added as extra input channels to the head, and the learned output weights from the first candidate. Choosing a safe placement order (for example, filling cells under an overhang first) needs information from beyond a 7x7 receptive field. The compute ratio is about 1.5, so fewer samples. Refuted if it does not beat r3c1's 0.11.
entries.last_analysis: r3c1 is the only trial with any successes. It sums the placement output over all 8 flips and transposes of the grid and scored 0.111 (0.078 and 0.145 on its two seeds). r3c3 used the same network and recipe with only the described action layout and scored 0.000. So the action layout probably differs from the description by a flip or transpose. Every trial without the flipped and transposed outputs scored 0, whatever the recipe or capacity, so those earlier zeros say little about recipes or network size. Training success (0.12) is close to dev success, which suggests the network is underfitting rather than overfitting. r3c1 trained in only 28 seconds. All three candidates keep the flipped and transposed outputs and change one thing each: a learned weight on each output so the wrong orientations can be switched off quickly, a recipe that gives more credit to the exact-build bonus, and a third residual block plus whole-board context in the head.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so all I know is that every trial ran. The 1-epoch recipe (r2c1) gave 3x the default's environment steps and stayed inside the time limit, and so did networks up to 1.89x the starting compute. On this task the main thing should be how fast fresh designs are seen and how precisely each footprint's landing height is read. Neither seed noise nor scores can be judged from what I have. This last round should combine plausible pieces, not open new axes. (1) The richest network so far (dilated trunk with context heads) with a longer-horizon recipe, so the final +1 bonus gets more credit. (2) The deep-column network with the same longer horizon. (3) A new head idea: a learned convolution the size of each footprint over projected features. It sees each cell under the brick separately, not just the max, min and mean.

entries.label: r4c3
entries.name: Shared shift kernel, 2 epochs
entries.hypothesis: Combines the shared shift kernel (candidate 1) with 2 PPO epochs. In r3c1, 2 epochs reached 0.77 on one seed but failed on the other, which looks like a slow, seed-dependent discovery of the shift. If a shared 8-weight shift makes alignment fast and reliable, both seeds should get the benefit of about 1.9x the samples. Refuted if mean dev success is not above 0.43, or if one seed again stays below 0.15.
entries.last_analysis: Realigning the shifted target with a learned wrap-around full-row convolution is what made learning possible (the starting net and the transformer both stayed at 0). The cheap early-fusion version, r2c2, is best at 0.43 (0.31 and 0.54). r3c1 uses the same net with 2 PPO epochs and scored about the same mean (0.42), but one seed reached 0.77 and the other only 0.08. More samples can therefore help a lot, but early learning is unreliable. Three changes did not help, within seed noise: the relative DONE logit, a longer horizon (gamma 0.99, which clearly hurt) and the footprint-convolution head. Higher entropy (0.02) went with a full collapse to DONE in both round-1 trials that used it. The failures look like slow or unlucky discovery of the shift early in training. So this round tests a shared shift kernel that should make alignment faster and more reliable, plus a middle ground of 3 PPO epochs.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: realign + more updates
entries.hypothesis: Same network as c1; only the recipe changes: 128 envs x 16 steps, 8 minibatches, 3 PPO epochs. This gives about 1.3x more samples (about 170k steps) and about 83 updates instead of 32, so the policy has more chances to learn rewarding placements before DONE dominates. Refuted if dev success is not above c1 by more than seed noise (about 5 points), or if it falls below c1.
entries.last_analysis: Undoing the observed X/2 column roll took dev success from 0 to 0.47, and r2c2's recipe (128 envs, 8 minibatches, 3 epochs) raised it to 0.715 on both seeds. Every change in round 3 lost ground: 64 envs, 2 epochs and a deeper trunk. All three had one seed at 0.000 and the other at 0.15–0.51. So the main problem is seed instability or collapse, not capacity or sample count. One collapse type: r3c1 seed 0 used only 1x1 bricks. Remaining errors in the traces are wrong-layer placements and stopping with DONE one brick short. For the last round I keep r2c2 and make one change per candidate: (A) near-uniform initial policy logits (small-gain output layers), so early exploration is unbiased; (B) a larger entropy bonus to resist collapse; (C) a longer horizon (gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95), so the +1 exact-build bonus outweighs per-step shaping and wrong-layer errors cost more.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis:
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. They covered pooled, 3x3, transformer and flatten heads, 1 to 4 PPO epochs and up to 426k steps. Training success never left zero for any network, including the head that makes no assumption about how actions map to cells. So the shared bottleneck is probably the recipe or exploration, not the network.

Every trial kept lr 1e-3. All but the starting run used entropy 0.003, and nothing tried entropy above 0.01. A likely failure mode is early collapse onto DONE or onto a few safe placements: random placements tend to fill cells outside the target, which costs reward, while DONE costs nothing. If the policy collapses there, it never reaches an exact build and never sees the +1 bonus. Gamma 0.95 also discounts that terminal bonus.

This last round tests the untried settings: higher entropy, a longer horizon, a lower learning rate and a higher one, and a wider receptive field.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: Conv head + global context
entries.hypothesis: This builds on r1c2's footprint-conv head. It adds a third residual conv with dilation 2 for a wider view, and broadcasts a global pooled vector back into every cell before the head. Placement scores can then depend on the state of the whole build, such as which regions are finished or must be built first. Uses r1c1's longer-horizon recipe; r is about 1.5. Refuted if it scores no better than r1c2 or the starting architecture.
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only compare candidates on priors. All 9 trials trained without errors, and no file ran close to the compute or time limits. Three directions look plausible. (1) Spend the budget on more fresh designs: fewer PPO epochs, gamma 0.99, gae_lambda 0.95. (2) Use footprint-shaped learned convolutions in the action head. (3) Use per-layer heads that reason about the landing layer and the cells a brick seals below it, with a running maximum over lower layers. Global context broadcast (r2c2) was only tested together with a costly dilated conv and the 4-epoch recipe. With one round left, the best use of the trials is to combine parts that each looked sound under the high-sample recipe, and to push that recipe one step further (1 epoch, about 3x the samples). Each trial changes one main thing relative to a trial it can be compared with.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: Flip-only big batch + stem skip
entries.hypothesis: r3c2 recipe plus the r3c3 stem skip. The footprint head also gets the flipped, unblurred per-cell stem features, so pooled max and min can match landing layers to missing cells more sharply. Large batches should keep both seeds stable. Refuted if the mean is no higher than 0.823, or if either seed drops clearly below 0.80.
entries.last_analysis: The key finding is alignment. Any version that keeps the unflipped stem (RowMix, Mixer, concat of flipped and unflipped, or a flip only in the head) collapsed to immediate DONE in most seeds. Mirroring the learned stem features along X before the 3x3 convolutions (flip-only) made both seeds escape the collapse in every run, so later layers work in landing coordinates. With 128 envs and 2,048-sample batches, r3c2 reached 0.844 and 0.803 (mean 0.823). The small-batch run of the same network (r3c1) spread from 0.26 to 0.80, so larger batches seem to reduce seed luck. The stem skip to the head (r3c3, 0.62 against 0.53 at small batch) is within noise but may help. Training success was still rising at the end of every run, so learning is short of samples and the network should stay small. In this last round each candidate refines r3c2 with one change: the stem skip, longer credit assignment (gamma and GAE lambda), or 3 PPO epochs to collect more samples.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: best + 2 epochs, more samples
entries.hypothesis: Change: same network and n_envs 128 as r1c2, but ppo_epochs drops from 4 to 2. That nearly doubles the sample budget (about 234k steps, about 114 updates). Fresh random designs may be worth more than reusing old ones, and it also gives more updates. Refuted if dev success is at or below the 0.87 of r1c2 with 4 epochs, which would mean reusing samples matters more.
entries.last_analysis: Mirroring the head along x fixed the starting architecture's 0.0 result. Seed-0 traces confirm that action x fills columns X-dx-x to X-1-x. On top of that head, recipe changes mattered most. Doubling updates (r1c2, 0.87) beat the default recipe (0.71). Two PPO epochs (r2c2, 0.927) beat four. The global-context head (r2c3, 0.913) is within noise of the best. The main risk is training collapse. Early random placements earn negative reward while DONE earns 0, so some seeds learn to end every episode at once: one r3c1 seed and both r3c3 seeds. One epoch instead fell into using only 1x1 bricks. More aggressive updates seem to raise this risk: one epoch, or minibatches of 1,024 samples with two epochs. A deeper trunk lost too many samples. For this last round I keep r2c2 and change one thing in each candidate: more entropy against collapse and ruts, a longer horizon for the exact-build bonus, or three epochs.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev and on training success. They differed widely in heads (per-layer, relational, pooled, flat MLP, dense), recipes (1, 2 or 4 epochs, 64 or 256 envs, up to 426k samples) and sizes. Seed noise cannot explain a flat zero this consistent. So a factor shared by all of them is the bottleneck. Two explanations fit. First, the dense reward rewards filling target cells even when a placement seals missing cells below it. The agent then learns greedy filling and never reaches the rare +1 for an exact build, which gamma 0.95 discounts further. Second, the world may differ from its description, for example a different anchor convention, swapped brick orientations or a transposed index. Then every head that assumes top-left anchoring is misaligned, and the flat heads may just learn too slowly. This last round tests both: a head that does not assume alignment and also sees the mask, the same head plus a dense path, and a baseline with a longer horizon.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only reason about the design. Every trial trained without errors, so the time limit and compute cap are not binding at these sizes. Over three rounds the search explored two kinds of change. On the recipe side it tried fewer PPO epochs with more fresh samples, and a longer horizon (gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95) to carry the exact-build bonus back to early placements. On the architecture side it tried per-layer heads (logsumexp, then a landing-gated version), layer attention, and a deeper dilated trunk with global context. The strongest recipe idea, 1 epoch with 512 envs at long horizon, has only been tested on the starting network. The structural heads have only used 2 epochs with about 135k samples. Since this is the last round and the final pick goes to the best 2-seed score, the best bets pair the most promising structures with the data-heavy recipe, plus one low-risk recipe refinement on the starting network.

entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: slim stem, compute ratio about 1
entries.hypothesis: Only change from r3c2: the stem shrinks (STEM 64 to 32, COL 48 to 40), bringing the compute ratio from about 1.21 to about 1.0. That gives about 20% more fresh samples and gradient steps. r3c2's curve was still rising, and widening the stem (r2c2) gave no clear gain, so stem width looks cheap to cut. Refuted if 2-seed dev success is at or below about 0.87, which would mean the stem's capacity mattered more than the extra samples.
entries.last_analysis: The circular full-row stem is what made learning possible, because it lets each cell see the target shifted 4 columns away. Without it, or with the learned column warp in r1c3, every trial collapsed to choosing DONE on the first step. Adding global context to the placement head helped (0.70 to 0.74). Recipe changes have mattered most since then. 64 minibatches gave 0.78. Using 1 epoch with 64 minibatches (r3c2) gave 0.89, with both seeds close (0.887 and 0.897). So the run is short of samples, and its learning curve was still rising at the end (0.77 to 0.82). The full footprint conv (r3c3, 0.54) and the wider stem (r2c2, 0.715 against 0.697) did not help, which suggests extra per-cell capacity is not the bottleneck. This is the last round, so all three candidates keep r3c2's architecture and recipe. One makes the network cheaper so that the training-compute ratio r is about 1, for about 20% more samples. One raises gamma so the +1 bonus for an exact build counts for more. The third combines both.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: half-roll, 1 epoch, lr 0.002
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c1 (1 PPO epoch), with lr going from 0.001 to 0.002. In r3c1, training success was only 0.09 at 25% of the run. A higher starting lr, which decays linearly, should shorten that slow start and leave more of the run for refinement. lr 0.002 was stable with 2 epochs (0.928). If dev success falls below about 0.91, or one seed collapses, 0.001 is better with 1 epoch.
entries.last_analysis: Rolling the target by X/2 along x was the key fix: it took dev success from 0 to 0.59. After that, the best lever was trading PPO epochs for more fresh samples: 4 epochs gave 0.59, 2 gave 0.90 and 1 gave 0.9355, the current best. lr 0.002 with 2 epochs scored 0.928, about the same as lr 0.001 within noise. A deeper or wider trunk hurt both times (0.56 and 0.34), probably because its extra FLOPs cut the sample count. r3c1's training curve flattened at about 0.91 over the last quarter. The remaining failures are probably DONE timing and stacking order. This is the last round, so all three candidates keep r3c1's network and 1 PPO epoch and change one thing each: a higher learning rate, a longer return horizon so the +1 exact-build bonus gets more credit, and feeding global context back into each cell's features.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0, on dev and in training, across very different heads (pooled, layer-gated, footprint-gather, dihedral, dense FC, per-action attention). So the bottleneck is probably not how actions map to cells. The likely causes are learning speed and precision. An exact build needs roughly 10 to 30 correct placements in a row, then DONE at exactly the right moment, and every run so far had only 32 to 120 policy updates. Recipe space is barely explored: only 2- and 4-epoch runs with 128 or 256 envs. The program says ppo_epochs=1 gives about 3.25x more environment steps, and that is untested. DONE has always been scored from weak mean/max pooling of trunk features. A learned per-cell projection followed by amax could better detect "anything still missing". This last round bets on more samples and policy updates, a sharper DONE and value signal, small-init output layers, and one global-attention variant.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: global trunk + per-layer head
entries.hypothesis: Feeds the r1c2 trunk (dilated residual convolution plus a broadcast global vector, so every cell sees the whole grid) into the r1c3 per-layer footprint head. Each layer's score can then depend on global build progress and on what is still missing elsewhere, which matters for build order. The per-layer head keeps landing-layer reasoning explicit. Compute is about 1.4x. Refuted if it scores at or below both r1c2 and r1c3.
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that every trial trained without errors. No result has been refuted. Two ideas in the plan are layer-relative: scoring placements separately for each layer and taking a logsumexp over layers, and using relative-height inputs. Both fit the task, because whether a brick is correct depends on its landing layer, the cells below it that it would seal, and the cells above it that it would block. Using 2 PPO epochs gives nearly twice the fresh designs at about the same number of gradient steps. With only 3 trials left, I keep the r2c3 design (layer-mixing, 2 epochs) as the anchor and make one change in each candidate: (a) a lower entropy bonus, since evaluation is greedy and the action space is large; (b) the relative z-window input from r3c3 combined with layer-mixing; (c) per-layer features fed into the DONE and value heads, so stopping can depend on whether a good placement remains. With 2 seeds and possible seed-luck failures, small differences will be hard to separate.

entries.label: r3c2
entries.name: flip after stem, 64 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same network as the flip-after-stem candidate, but with n_minibatches 64 instead of 32. With one epoch, this doubles the gradient steps per sample (64-sample minibatches). Training success levelled off at about 0.85 while the learning rate decayed, so more optimiser steps on the same fresh data should extract more from each sample. Refuted if this is not clearly above the plain flip-after-stem candidate, or if one seed becomes unstable.
entries.last_analysis: The left-right mirror rule is the main obstacle. A fixed flip (in the head, or right after the stem) unlocks learning. A learned column mixer collapsed to DONE. After that, the recipe matters most: going from 2 PPO epochs to 1 means more fresh samples (0.84 to 0.92), and 64 minibatches give more gradient steps per sample (0.897 to 0.949 for the flip-after-stem net). Extra depth hurts: it costs samples, and one deeper seed collapsed to 0.08. gamma 0.99 was unstable. At the best trial's end, training success was still rising (0.91), so the remaining gains probably come from better use of samples or cheap context, not bigger trunks. Seed spread at the top is about ±0.01–0.02, so gains under about 0.02 are not reliable. For this final round I make one change each to the best trial r3c2: a higher learning rate, broadcast global context into the placement head, and a dilated second convolution for a wider view at the same compute.

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: r1c2 with lr 2e-3
entries.hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r1c2, but with learning rate 2e-3 instead of 1e-3. r1c2's training curve was still rising at the end (0.85 to 0.88). Because the rate decays linearly to 0, the last part of training makes small steps, and doubling the rate should finish the job at the same budget. Refuted if dev success is not above 0.913 by more than about 0.03, or if a seed falls into the DONE trap.
entries.last_analysis: Placing logits at the cell each action actually fills (the mirrored head) is what made learning possible. It took dev success from 0 to 0.75–0.94. The best recipe so far uses 128 envs and 3 epochs. A 64-env recipe with 1 or 2 epochs made seeds fall into the trap of choosing DONE first: r2c2 lost both seeds, r2c1 lost one, and r2c3 lost both, so r2c3's architecture result is confounded with that recipe. Raising lr to 2e-3 helped a little: 0.9375 against 0.913, a difference inside the noise, but both seeds were good and the curve was still rising. Adding raw observations to the head did nothing. A separate critic hurt (0.52), so the shared critic seems helpful. The remaining failures are a few cells placed outside the target and stopping too early, which point to how the discount treats the end of the episode and to the lack of global context. This last round tests a higher discount, a higher learning rate, and a cheap global broadcast with the safe recipe.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0, in training as well as on dev. That includes recipe sweeps over epochs, entropy, lr and gamma, a deeper trunk, a per-layer network, a dihedral gate and a dense action remap. If the world matched its description, a 1x1 policy that places bricks on target cells at the landing layer should learn quickly and build some small designs exactly. A hard zero everywhere therefore points to a mismatch between the network's outputs and the env's action layout, not to capacity or recipe. Ruled out so far: flips and transpositions with type-major order and DONE last, and per-type anchor or footprint offsets, which the 3x3 heads covered. Not yet tested: other orderings of the type/y/x axes in the action index (for example type-minor), and DONE sitting at index 0. If DONE sits at index 0, the agent can never stop, so success is impossible. This last round covers these with cheap output-side gates plus a per-action global term, and adds a layout-free attention head as a hedge.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only choose from priors and from which trials trained cleanly. All 9 trials trained without errors. The layer-aware landing head is the idea that best matches the task: whether a placement is right depends on which layer the brick lands in and whether that layer is missing cells there. Its latest version, r3c1, adds z-cumulative features and a landing gate. It uses about 1.5x the starting compute and trains for 278k steps, well inside the time and compute limits. Recipes that see more fresh designs (1 epoch, 512 envs) give 2–3x more samples. That should help generalisation to unseen designs. In this final round I refine r3c1 in three ways, one main change each: (1) the legal-action mask as a learned input to the head, (2) cheap per-layer spatial context from a depthwise 3x3 conv, and (3) a recipe change to 32-step rollouts with lower entropy.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: shift gate + entropy 0.05
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c3, but the entropy coefficient rises from 0.03 to the maximum, 0.05. Raising it from 0.01 to 0.03 lifted the weak seed from collapse to 0.23 (full stack) and to 0.61 (gate). More entropy should delay the early collapse onto DONE further, so the weak seed reaches seed 0's level of about 0.84. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is not above 0.72, or if seed 0 falls clearly below 0.8.
entries.last_analysis: Every model that learned anything uses some way of undoing the target shift: a stack of shifted copies or a learned shift gate. Without it, the agent quickly learns to choose DONE before placing anything. Seed 0 seems to top out at about 0.84 under any reasonable setup. Seed 1 decides the mean: across trials it scored 0.31, 0.60, 0, 0, 0, 0.23, 0.08 and 0.61. The best result, r3c3 (0.72), is the shared shift gate plus entropy 0.03, the only setup where seed 1 got above 0.6. Its training success was still rising at the end. Things that hurt stability: 64 envs (both seeds collapsed) and 2 PPO epochs (one seed collapsed). With 128 envs both seeds survived. The useful moves are those that make seed 1 align faster or collapse later. All three candidates keep r3c3 and change one thing: a stronger entropy bonus, more parallel worlds per update at the same number of updates, or more gate mixtures.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: roll, 2 epochs, lr 0.002
entries.hypothesis: Same as r2c1, but lr is 0.002 instead of 0.001. Training success was still rising at the end while the learning rate decayed to zero. At 3 epochs, lr 0.002 raised final training success (0.86 against 0.81). Combined with the extra samples from 2 epochs, it should finish more of the learning curve and score above 0.94. Refuted if dev success falls below about 0.90 or a seed collapses.
entries.last_analysis: The observed target is shifted cyclically by X/2. Undoing that shift is the only architecture change that worked: every run with it either reached about 0.85–0.94 dev success or fell to near 0 by seed luck. Fewer PPO epochs helped. 3 epochs gave 0.888 and 2 epochs gave 0.937, the best so far (r2c1). With 1 epoch the agent used only 1x1 bricks, which cannot form overhangs, and scored 0.077. Doubling the learning rate at 3 epochs gave about 0.89, the same as before. Adding the stem features to the footprint head (0.907) was within noise of the best. The main risk is that one seed collapses, either to pressing DONE or to the 1x1-only habit, as with gamma 0.99 and with all x-shifts as input. At 2 epochs r2c1's training success was still rising at the end (0.894 to 0.926), so the agent has not finished learning. Because this is the last round, all three candidates keep r2c1's network and change one recipe setting each.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on both seeds, and training success was also 0. That held across recipes (1, 2 and 4 epochs; lr, entropy and gamma changes) and across heads (footprint pooling, layer-resolved, footprint-concat, dense, transformer). A policy that is merely weak should still build a few 6-brick designs exactly. A flat 0 instead suggests a structural mismatch: this world probably decodes actions differently from the stated layout. It might transpose or flip y and x, order actions cell-first instead of type-first, or put DONE first. Local convolutional heads cannot learn such a remapping. The dense and positional-transformer heads could learn it in principle, but probably too slowly with about 250k samples. So in this last round, every candidate scores several possible action layouts at once and sums them. Each layout gets its own small learned output map, so training can strengthen the correct one and shrink the others toward zero.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that every trial trained without errors and stayed well inside the caps. Prior expectations still matter. Training designs are random and endless, so fresh data should help generalisation, which favours fewer epochs and more samples. The exact-build bonus comes at the end of the episode, which favours gamma 0.98 and lambda 0.95. The cheapest wins come from recipe changes on the cheap baseline network, because a bigger network costs samples. This is the last round, and all trials compete for selection. So I combine the changes most likely to help into three different candidates. (1) r3c1 with twice as many gradient steps per update, because 1 epoch with 16 minibatches gives only about 1,600 gradient steps in total. (2) The deeper context network on the r3c1 recipe. (3) The baseline at 2 epochs with the long-horizon settings, as a middle point between sample reuse and fresh data.

entries.label: r2c3
entries.name: flipped trunk, 128 updates
entries.hypothesis: Uses the flipped-trunk network with n_envs 64 and 8 minibatches of 128 samples. That gives about 128 updates, against 64 in r1c3. In round 1, going from 32 to 64 updates raised dev success from 0.70 to 0.90, so halving the batch again may speed learning further. Refuted if it scores clearly below the flipped trunk at 64 updates (the other proposal), which would mean the batches are now too small and too noisy.
entries.last_analysis: Lining the features up with the mirrored landing columns was the decisive change. Without it the starting network scored 0. A fixed flip scored 0.70 to 0.93, and a learned column remap reached only 0.10. After that, the recipe mattered most. Going from 32 to 64 updates raised success from 0.70 to 0.90. r2c3 (flipped trunk, 64 worlds, 4 epochs, about 128 updates) is best at 0.928. r2c1 (2 epochs, 128 worlds) and r2c2 (flipped trunk, 64 updates) both scored about 0.92, the same within noise. In round 3, every run that used 2 epochs with 64 worlds (about 236 small updates) collapsed to DONE on both seeds, or nearly so. That includes the deeper-trunk and global-context runs, so those two ideas were never properly tested. Their recipe was the confound. Safe recipes so far use at least about 2k samples per update or 4 epochs. Remaining errors are probably wrong ordering under overhangs or stopping at the wrong time (IoU 0.989 against 0.92 success).

entries.label: r1c2
entries.name: flip + more updates
entries.hypothesis: Same flip alignment, but with a recipe for more and smaller updates: ppo_epochs 2 gives about 1.86x the samples, and n_envs 128 gives about 119 updates instead of 32. The default budget allows only 32 PPO updates, which is probably too few to escape the early DONE attractor and learn building order. Refuted if this scores clearly below the plain flip candidate by more than the seed noise.
entries.last_analysis: The biggest gain came from flipping the trunk features along x so they line up with the action grid: 0 → 0.745. The second came from making more, smaller PPO updates (2 epochs, 128 envs, 113 updates): 0.943. Settings near this recipe are fragile. One PPO epoch, 64 envs and a 1.35x-FLOP network each led to collapse on one or both seeds, usually into an early-DONE or low-success state. So fewer updates, noisier updates and fewer samples are all risky. lr 0.002 (0.941) and global context in the head (0.926) were within noise of the best. Gamma 0.99 gave the best single seed (0.953) but made seeds unstable. Dev IoU is about 0.99, so the remaining failures are small precision or ordering errors. This last round keeps the r1c2 recipe and FLOPs and tests three things: cheap per-cell precision (a stem skip into the head), a sharper policy for greedy evaluation (lower entropy coefficient), and a moderate longer horizon.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 in training. That covers the baseline conv net, recipes with 1 or 2 epochs, deeper trunks, per-layer heads, dense remapping heads, a transformer and a flat MLP. Because the MLP and the dense heads also failed, a mismatch between the action grid and the observation grid is unlikely to be the only cause. The common factor is the recipe. Every run used gamma 0.95 or 0.97, entropy 0.005 to 0.01, and either 2 epochs with batch 2048 or 1 epoch with batch 4096. No run tested high gamma, high entropy, small batches or many updates. The remaining bottlenecks are probably exploration and credit assignment: the +1 exact-build bonus and a correctly timed DONE are far apart and rare. With only success numbers to go on, I cannot tell which hidden twist applies. This last round therefore spends the trials on untested recipe settings (gamma 0.99, entropy 0.02 to 0.03, smaller and more frequent updates) and on one new trunk with a wider view of the board.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so the trials can't be ranked. All nine trained without errors, and the two-seed noise is unknown. The search covered three families of ideas: recipes with more frequent updates (fewer envs, 1–3 epochs, gamma 0.97, lambda 0.95), placement heads that model the brick (learned footprint convolution, per-layer logsumexp head), and global attention. This is the last round, so each proposal combines parts that already train cleanly into a plausible best candidate. One gives the footprint-conv head the 1-epoch, ~400k-sample recipe (r3c2's recipe). One adds a cheap dilated residual conv to the footprint-conv model, which widens the receptive field without the cost of attention. One gives the per-layer head the 1-epoch recipe. All stay near 1–1.4x compute so they finish well inside the time limit. No result will tell me which recipe was better, because the scores are hidden, but the final selection uses the real dev scores.

entries.label: r1c3
entries.name: attention with wrap-around bias
entries.hypothesis: Inserts one multi-head self-attention layer over all cells after the stem, before the 3x3 trunk. Each head has a learned position bias indexed by row offset and by column offset with wrap-around; the bias starts at zero and is scaled up so it can learn quickly. Heads can learn to attend 3, 4 or 5 columns over, bringing in target features. The recipe matches the second candidate. If it scores clearly below the second candidate, attention learns the shift too slowly for this budget.
entries.last_analysis: Aligning the shifted target is the key: none of 0, wrap-around row conv 0.65, wrap-around attention 0.81. Most of the gap between runs is seed collapse into early DONE, not skill. r2c1 scored 0.87 on one seed and 0 on the other; both seeds of r2c2 collapsed, as did one seed of r3c2. Runs that survive score about 0.75–0.88. Entropy 0.02 did not stop collapse. A second attention block and split stems both slowed learning. Collapse happens because random placements cost reward until the shift is learned. So the most promising levers are (a) learning the alignment faster: attention values taken by a linear map straight from the raw observation, so the shifted target arrives intact, and (b) a standard near-uniform policy start (small output-layer init), so DONE gets no early lead. Last round: test each lever alone on r1c3, plus both together.

entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: r3c1 + 16 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: This keeps r3c1's 119 updates of 1024 samples but splits each update into 16 minibatches of 64 instead of 8 of 128. That doubles the gradient steps per update at the same compute. More optimisation steps has been the most reliable lever so far. Expect a mean above 0.90. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.87 or a seed collapses, which would mean the smaller, noisier minibatches destabilise PPO.
entries.last_analysis:
The target channels are shifted by X/2 along x. Rolling them back fixed the collapse to DONE (0.00 to 0.59). The recipe then mattered most: going from 256 to 128 envs (twice the updates, plus entropy 0.03) raised success to 0.86, and 64 envs reached 0.90 with both seeds near 0.89. Training success was still rising at the end. More update steps in the same budget keeps helping.
Several changes did not help:
- Adding parameters (dilated trunk at 0.62, landing head at 0.81) cost training steps and lost.
- 2 PPO epochs left one seed collapsed. 3 epochs (0.865) changed nothing.
- gamma 0.99 (0.83) changed nothing.
- A learned axis remap never escaped the collapse.
Dev IoU is about 0.985, so the remaining failures are small errors.
For the final round, keep the r3c1 network. Test three ways to get more or larger optimisation steps per sample: shorter rollouts (more updates), more minibatches (more gradient steps per update), and a higher learning rate.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and also on training (sampled) success. That held across three architecture families and recipes from 120k to 400k steps. The world probably differs from the description in a way that local convolutions cannot absorb. The flat linear head was too weak to compensate, and more samples, entropy changes and a DONE redesign did nothing. Remapping channels is already learnable through the 1x1 stems. Anchor shifts of about one cell were covered by the 3x3 heads in r3c2. Two causes remain untested: a spatial mismatch between the observation grid and the action grid (transpose or flip), and a more arbitrary cell mapping. The last round tests both. One candidate adds explicit flipped and transposed copies of the features to the head. One uses attention with learned positions, which can learn any mapping. One combines the two. Any nonzero score beats the baseline.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible. Every trial trained cleanly, so nothing here can be ranked on evidence; only reasoning separates them. Three things should help. First, the per-layer footprint features fit the drop rule. Second, fewer PPO epochs buy more fresh designs (2 epochs gives about 1.8x the samples) and more updates, which should help on held-out designs. Third, build-wide context should help with placement order. r3c3 combines all three. Its 1.17x compute keeps it fast, so it is the base for this round. As this is the last round, I chose three candidates that differ in kind so the final selection has distinct options: (a) push the sample-count idea to 1 epoch; (b) use a longer reward horizon for the exact-build bonus, plus less entropy so greedy play is sharper; (c) feed the legality mask and the layer above each cell into the network, so it can see overhang and height-limit structure.

entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: r3c1 with 32 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c1, but n_minibatches is 32 instead of 16. This doubles the gradient steps per update (64 instead of 32) with smaller minibatches, at the same sample budget and compute. Training is limited by optimisation speed, so more steps per batch should help, as the higher lr did. Refuted if dev success is at most about 0.85.
entries.last_analysis: Mirroring the trunk features (flip-concat) and pooling them over each brick footprint is what lets the agent learn this world at all. Without it, or with a learned column remap (0.40), results are much weaker. The recipe matters a lot. Two PPO epochs gave 0.72, against 0.53 with four. One epoch collapsed into ending every episode with DONE straight away (0.00). Raising lr to 0.002 gave the best result, 0.89, with both seeds close together. A larger network costs samples and lost: a deeper trunk scored 0.56 and a wider head 0.48. A longer gamma made seeds unstable (0.30). The global-context head (0.76 vs 0.72) is within noise. r3c1's training curve was still rising at the end (0.72 to 0.83), so the agent is still limited by optimisation speed at this budget. In this final round I keep the r3c1 network and push optimisation speed: lr 0.003, more minibatch steps per update, and the global-context head combined with lr 0.002.

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: flip + 64 envs (more updates)
entries.hypothesis: Same network as r2c2, but n_envs drops 128 to 64 with 16 minibatches of 64 samples. That gives about 120 updates instead of 60 on the same number of samples. r2c2 was still improving and doubling updates gave +14 points, so learning looks limited by updates. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is not above 0.888 by more than about 0.03, or if the seeds diverge, since updates on fewer environments are noisier.
entries.last_analysis: The main gain came from flipping the feature map along x so that each anchor logit pools over the cells the brick actually fills. Without it, dev success was 0, and learning the mapping with axial mixing (r1c3) also scored 0. After that fix, the number of updates mattered most. With the same sample budget, dev success went from 0.745 (30 updates) to 0.888 (60) to 0.931 (about 120, n_envs 64), and both seeds of each run stayed close. Changes that cost samples or added instability did not help: the footprint-conv head (about equal), the dilated third conv (0.851) and lr 2e-3 (0.833). Seed noise looks like roughly ±0.03–0.05. The remaining failures are small: IoU is 0.995 and about 0.12 cells per episode land outside the target. n_envs is already at its minimum of 64, so this round halves rollout_len to 8 to double the updates again. It also tests trading one PPO epoch for more samples, and a lower entropy bonus, since evaluation is greedy.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored 0 on dev, and training success was also 0. That held across recipes (1, 2 and 4 epochs; gamma 0.95 to 0.99; entropy 0.002 to 0.01), per-layer heads, attention, dihedral and fully connected heads that ignore the action frame, and mask input. So a mismatch between the obs frame and the action frame is unlikely to be the cause. A sound guess is that training collapses early. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they earn negative reward. DONE earns 0, so PPO may learn to quit at once or to make safe, timid moves before it finds the placement rule. The remaining bets aim at early-stage dynamics: stronger and longer exploration, standard PPO initialisation (an almost uniform starting policy and a well-scaled critic), and a separate critic so value learning does not distort the policy features.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture

entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: 1 epoch, higher lr
entries.hypothesis: Same network as r3c1, with ppo_epochs 1 (about 367k samples) and lr raised from 0.001 to 0.002. One epoch moves the policy less per update; doubling the learning rate makes up for that and speeds the early escape from pressing DONE at once, while the larger sample count is kept. PPO clipping limits instability. Refuted if it scores clearly below the 1-epoch version at lr 0.001, or below r3c1's 0.699 by more than seed noise.
entries.last_analysis: Every trial without a circular row convolution on the target channels scored 0: the agent learned to press DONE at once. The circular (1, X) convolution unlocked learning (r2c1: 0.447). The generic axial version (0.325) and ent_coef 0.05 (0.339) were no better, given the seed noise. Halving PPO epochs from 4 to 2 nearly doubled the samples and gave the clearest gain (r3c1: 0.699, training success still rising at 0.675). So the run is short of samples, not of optimisation per sample. The missing/extra pooling for the DONE head did not help (0.404, and 0.297 with 2 epochs, where one seed scored 0.078). Seed spread is large, up to about 0.44 between seeds. In this final round I push the sample-count lever further, to 1 PPO epoch (about 367k steps), and test a higher learning rate and more frequent smaller updates on top of it. The architecture stays fixed at r3c1, the best so far.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: Shifted input, 1 PPO epoch
entries.hypothesis: Same as r1c1, but with ppo_epochs 1. That gives about 3.25x the samples (about 425k steps) for a similar number of gradient steps. Together with the 2-epoch trial it shows which way to move on epochs. Fresh, varied designs should generalise better to held-out targets than reusing data. Refuted if it scores below both the 2-epoch candidate and r1c1 (about 0.59), which would mean one epoch learns too little from each sample.
entries.last_analysis: The X/2 input shift makes the task learnable. Moving to 1 PPO epoch for about 3x more samples gave the best result: r2c2 at 0.936, with both seeds high. Most failures now come from a few unlucky seeds. Three runs scored exactly 0.0781 on one seed. Where readouts exist, the agent fills only the ground layer, then picks DONE (IoU 0.714). Bad seeds appear with more gradient steps per sample (r3c1) and longer horizons (gamma 0.99 in r3c3, which picked DONE at once). A bigger trunk cost samples and hurt (r3c2). The remaining gains likely come from making early training reliable, not from more capacity. So each candidate makes one change to r2c2 aimed at stable early learning: lower gamma, near-zero starting action scores (a standard initialisation), or fewer, larger minibatches.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success in the last 10% of training was also 0. The changes covered three recipes (3 epochs, 1 epoch with high samples, and low gamma with low lr), three trunks (a CNN, layer tokens and a transformer) and three heads (footprint pooling, a learned 3x3 conv and multi-anchor pooling). A uniform zero across such different designs points to a shared assumption, not to capacity or recipe. Every head so far assumes that action index = type*Y*X + y*X + x and maps the logits spatially onto the grid. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. If the action layout or footprint geometry differs, for example cell-major order, transposed axes or reordered types, every spatial head is wrong. This round tests heads that assume no action geometry: a fully connected head to all actions, with the legality mask fed in through a learned linear layer, so the network can learn the real layout.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so the evidence is only that every design trained without error and stayed within the time limit. The final pick will go to the highest 2-seed dev score. Since this is the last round, the most useful candidates are strong combinations of ideas that each had a sound reason behind them. Those ideas are: more fresh samples (fewer PPO epochs), a longer credit horizon for the bonus that arrives only at episode end, global context, and the per-layer footprint head that matches how bricks land. The global-context trunk is the cheapest network (about 1.04x compute), so it can see the most data. The per-layer head is the best match to the task's structure but has never been tested with a longer horizon or with any spatial mixing inside each layer. I propose: (1) the 1-epoch global-context net plus gamma 0.98; (2) the per-layer head plus gamma 0.98; (3) the per-layer head plus a 3x3 convolution inside each layer, so it can see neighbouring support and overhang structure at that layer.

entries.label: r2c1
entries.name: Flip, 2 PPO epochs
entries.hypothesis: Same network and recipe as the best trial, but with ppo_epochs set to 2. This buys about 1.85x more environment steps (about 118 updates). Training success was still rising at the end, so the agent looks sample-limited, and fresh data should help it generalise to new designs more than extra passes over old data. Refuted if dev success is not above 0.864 by more than about 3 points, or if the training curve flattens earlier.
entries.last_analysis: The flip of the column axis is what made learning possible: 0 without it, 0.64–0.94 with it, and learned column mixing without it reached only 0.04. Among recipes, 2 PPO epochs is best so far (r2c1, 0.941, seeds 0.949 and 0.934). 4 epochs gave 0.864, and 1 epoch lost a seed (0.934 and 0.000), so too many updates risk instability. A longer horizon (gamma 0.99) scored 0.902 with 2 epochs. Extra trunk depth plus global broadcast (0.711) and the per-cell verify head (0.856) both did worse; their extra compute cost samples. Going from 64 to 128 updates helped in round 1. Remaining dev failures are rare order or overhang errors (about 0.14 cells outside the target per episode). This is the last round, so two candidates are single-change recipe refinements of r2c1 and one is a cheap new architecture idea with unchanged compute.

entries.label: r2c3
entries.name: 2 epochs, longer credit horizon
entries.hypothesis: Same network and 2-epoch recipe as r1c3, with gamma 0.99 and gae_lambda 0.95 instead of 0.95 and 0.9. Episodes run about 10 to 16 placements, so with gamma 0.95 the +1 for an exact build is heavily discounted at early steps. A longer horizon should give more credit to finishing exactly and less to stopping early. Refuted if dev success is no better than r1c3 (0.73) or if training becomes less stable.
entries.last_analysis: Flipping the features along x (the mirror fix) is what made learning possible. Fewer PPO epochs, and so more samples, helped: r2c1 used 1 epoch and scored 0.86 on both seeds. r2c3 (2 epochs, gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95) is the best at 0.90. All three round-3 failures got stuck in the same way. Each has a seed scoring 0.078, mean IoU 0.714 and 0 cells placed outside the target. They build only layer 0, never stack, then choose DONE. This early trap is a matter of seed luck, not of capacity. The 1-epoch long-horizon run (r3c1) reached 0.83 on its other seed. The dilated conv cut the step count and gave no clear gain. So with only 3 trials left, I make small changes to r2c3 aimed at avoiding the ground-only trap. One gives more exploration, one gives credit over whole episodes instead of value bootstrapping, and one stops the critic from interfering with the DONE decision.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and also 0 on train success. That held across recipes (1, 2 and 4 epochs, entropy from 0.003 to 0.02), heads (pooled, footprint-conv, per-layer and dense) and the slow-DONE fix. Small differences are not what is going on: something stops any success at all. The task says the world may not behave as described, so the likeliest blocker is a mismatch between action indices and cells. Every aligned head assumes a top-left anchor and the stated y/x order. The dense head could have learned any mapping, but it probably learns too slowly on about 400k samples. A cheap hedge is a learned local window for each brick type: a 3x3 conv covers top-left, centred and bottom-right anchors, and adding transposed features covers a y/x swap. The legality mask also reveals the anchor convention and orientation, so feeding it in as an input should help. These are last-round bets aimed at getting any nonzero score.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I have to rely on priors and on what the trials cover. Every trial so far trained without errors. With the default recipe, the policy changes only about 32 times per run (4,096 samples per update). That is very few, and it is probably a stronger limit than the network. Of the networks tried, the stem-skip net (r2c2) is the cheapest refinement: it adds about 8% compute and sends sharp per-column information to the footprint head, which is the most direct route to judging where a brick lands and whether it matches the target. The per-cell head (r3c1) is a natural extension of it. In this last round I keep the networks known to train and change mainly the update schedule: half as many parallel worlds (128), so the policy updates more than twice as often. I also use a longer horizon (gamma 0.97 to 0.99), so the bonus for an exact build reaches back through the whole episode and the agent learns better when to choose DONE.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: slim aligned net, 3 epochs
entries.hypothesis: This is r3c3's slim network (compute about 1x the start) with 3 PPO epochs instead of 2. That gives about 168k steps, more than r2c3's 139k. Every 3-epoch run so far kept both seeds learning, while 2-epoch runs collapsed or stalled on one seed. So this should keep r3c3's sample advantage and lift the weak seed. Refuted if the mean is at or below r2c3's 0.47, or if one seed is still under 0.25.
entries.last_analysis: The cheap learned shift-align module beats the costly axial convolutions. Spending compute on samples rather than width helps: the slim r3c3 reached 0.71 on one seed with IoU 0.95. The main risk is the early drift toward DONE. Mean episode length at 25% of training is about 2, and it fully collapsed in r1c3 and r3c2 seed 0 (both 2 epochs or tiny batches). The slim 2-epoch run r3c3 also had one weak seed (0.19).
