Every 3-epoch run kept both seeds alive (0.55/0.38, 0.47/0.32). Entropy between 0.03 and 0.04 makes no difference within noise. So: (A) the slim net with the more reliable 3 epochs, which still gets about 168k steps; (B) the slim net with 2 epochs and zero-initialised policy and value outputs, so it starts from a uniform policy and does not depend on random output-layer init; (C) both, zero-init plus 3 epochs.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: stem-pooled done/value, 3 epochs
entries.hypothesis: The r2c3 network and recipe, but the DONE and value heads also get the mean and max over cells of the 1x1 stem features. These carry the aligned missing/extra cells for each layer, so 'any target cell still missing?' becomes nearly linear. That should stop early DONE and improve the critic. Refuted if the mean is not above 0.94 or a seed falls below 0.85.
entries.last_analysis: An x-shifted copy of the observation fixed a fixed X/2 misalignment between target channels and action coordinates (0 → 0.59). The stem-feature skip into the footprint head gave the best result (r2c3, 0.94). Recipe: 128 envs with 2–3 epochs beat the default, and batches of 1,024 collapsed to DONE. Runs are fragile: single seeds fell to 0.15 (r1c3, r3c1) and 0.45 (r3c2), so 2 vs 3 epochs is within noise. The weak r3c1 seed stopped too early (IoU 0.83, almost no cells outside the target, training success flat near 0.2); the weak r3c3 seed placed wrong cells. My guess: the DONE and value heads see only pooled post-3x3 features and do not reliably know whether target cells are still missing. Giving them pooled per-cell stem features (which carry missing/extra cells directly) should make stopping reliable and improve the critic. All three candidates add this, each with a different recipe.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored 0 on dev, and none built a single design exactly during training. That covers different recipes, trunks, per-layer scorers, dense heads and attention heads, so neither the network body nor the action layout looks like the bottleneck. A shared cause is more likely: the agent almost never chooses DONE. Every build overshoots, because any placement after completion adds extra cells, and the 33-placement limit never lines up with an exact finish. To succeed, the agent must choose DONE right after completion. But DONE is 1 logit among about 1,000 legal placements, so at the start it is sampled roughly 0.1% of the time. The entropy bonus over this large action space also pushes DONE's probability back toward about 1/1000. So the +1 bonus is never seen. All three candidates this round add a gated DONE head: p(DONE) comes from a sigmoid, and the placements share the remaining probability. Around that change they vary the entropy coefficient, the credit horizon and the trunk.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only reason about design. All 9 trials ran without errors. r3c2 (about 400k steps) shows that 1 PPO epoch with 512 envs fits within the time limit. Three ideas have each been tried at 2 or 3 epochs but never with 1 epoch: per-layer landing heads, cell attention, and more samples per unit of compute. Since this is the last round, I will put these ideas together rather than open new directions. A and B test whether attention or the landing head works best with lots of samples at 1 epoch. C combines both modules at 2 epochs, which hedges in case 1 epoch is too few gradient steps. For the 1-epoch runs I use 32 minibatches instead of 16, which doubles the gradient steps per update compared with r3c2.

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: Both orientations, 4x updates
entries.hypothesis: Same network as r2c2. n_envs drops to 64 with 16 minibatches of 64, giving about 118 updates instead of about 62 for the same compute. Going from 32 to 62 updates added 15 points, and the training curve was still rising at the end. Refuted if dev success is at or below about 0.84, the r2c2 score minus noise, which would mean the gradients are now too noisy or the update count no longer limits learning.
entries.last_analysis: Concatenating the trunk features with an X-flipped copy before the footprint head was the key change. It took dev success from 0 to 0.71, likely because pooling on the flipped copy covers the cells where the mirrored brick lands. After that, recipe changes that gave more updates and more gradient steps helped steadily: 0.71 with 32 updates, 0.86 with 62 and 0.93 with 118, with the two seeds within about 0.01 of each other. Training success was still rising at the end of r3c1. A deeper dilated trunk lost about 1.7x in samples and hurt both times. gamma 0.99 scored 0.82 against 0.86, which is within noise and not worth pursuing. Dev IoU is already 0.99, so what remains is small ordering and overhang errors. That calls for more and faster learning in the same compute, not a bigger network. All three candidates therefore keep r3c1's network and change one recipe knob each: fewer epochs for more fresh samples, shorter rollouts for more updates, or a higher learning rate.

entries.label: r3c3
entries.name: r2c1 with lr 2e-3
entries.hypothesis: Double the learning rate to 0.002 on r2c1's recipe. Learning is limited by speed: training success was 0.30 at 25% of training and still rising at the end. Linear decay to 0 should reduce late instability, and the 0.2 clip limits the size of each policy step. Refuted if dev success is at or below 0.919, or if the learning curve shows collapse or plateaus lower.
entries.last_analysis: Fixing the mirrored column mapping took dev success from 0 to 0.75. Updating more often helped next: 64 worlds scored 0.919 against 0.868 for 128. A learning rate of 0.002 gave the best, 0.926, within noise of 0.919 but with a faster early learning curve. Rollout length 8 and 2 PPO epochs each had one seed fail (0.30, 0.00), so they are unsafe for the 4-seed retrain. Gamma 0.99 gave a small, noise-level gain at 128 worlds and is untested on the best recipe. Bigger or slower heads lost because they get fewer samples (r1c3, r2c3). Greedy traces now fail mostly on ordering under overhangs. The head sees only 3x3-smoothed trunk features, which may blur the per-layer column information it needs to judge where a brick lands. Last round: two single changes to r3c3, plus their combination.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Nine trials all scored exactly 0 on dev, and none had any successful builds in the last 10% of training either. The failures span five architectures (footprint pooling, layer-resolved heads, a plain residual CNN, a transformer, a dense action head) and recipes with 1–2 epochs, gamma 0.95–0.99 and entropy 0.003–0.01. So no tested change mattered. The cause is probably something these runs share, not capacity. The reward per placement is dense, so a myopic policy should already do fairly well: it only needs to place the brick that fills missing cells and add no extras. Two settings were never tested: a short horizon with sharp exploitation (gamma 0.9, lambda 0.8, very low entropy), and a separate critic, so that value learning stops interfering with the policy features. In this last round, all three candidates use the myopic, low-entropy recipe on three different architectures, so a single positive result would point to the recipe.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only judge the trials by their design. All 8 trials trained without errors. The footprint-convolution head (r1c2) is the most direct way to see the cells under each footprint, so it is the base for every candidate here. Deeper trunks, attention and layer-wise scoring each raised r. That cuts the sample count, and since every episode uses a fresh random design, samples look like the scarce resource. Trials that kept r near 1.2 and used 1 to 2 PPO epochs (r2c2, r3c1, r3c3) seem the safest bets, but without scores I cannot rank them. With one round left I avoid risky architecture changes. I propose two low-variance recipe combinations that blend the sample-rich and low-entropy ideas, and one cheap network change: feeding the legal-action mask in as an input. The mask shows where the height limit blocks a placement, at almost no extra compute.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: best recipe, lr 0.0015
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c2 (256 envs, 1 epoch, entropy 0.03), with lr raised from 0.001 to 0.0015. With 256 envs, early learning was slow (0.07 training success at 25%) and success was still rising at the end, so the budget limits learning speed. Larger rollouts should keep the higher rate stable. Refuted if the mean falls below 0.864 by more than about 4 points, or if a seed collapses.
entries.last_analysis: Letting the target channels pass through a learned wrap-around convolution 1 row high and X columns wide is what made the task learnable. It took the start from 0.000 to above 0.76, while a dense mixing layer over each row reached only 0.42. Fewer PPO epochs, and so more fresh samples, helped: 4 epochs scored 0.77, 2 epochs 0.84, and 1 epoch gave seeds of 0.92 and 0.94. But 1 epoch with 128 envs left one seed collapsed (0.0 and 0.37). Raising to 256 envs (minibatches of 128 samples) with entropy 0.03 kept both seeds healthy, at 0.864 (0.90 and 0.83). That suggests noisy small-batch updates cause the collapse. These changes did not help: a deeper dilated trunk, a longer discount horizon, and a separate critic, which badly hurt. At the end of r3c2, training success was still rising and its early learning was slow (0.07 at 25% of training). So learning speed and stability now matter more than capacity. The traces suggest the remaining failures are a few cells placed in the wrong spot or in the wrong order.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: r2c1 with gamma 0.9
entries.hypothesis: Only change from r2c1: gamma goes from 0.95 to 0.9. Gamma 0.99 made seeds collapse to DONE because random early placements add up to a large negative return. A shorter horizon makes stopping early look less attractive, while each correct cell still pays straight away. The exact-build bonus is paid at the DONE step itself, so it is not discounted. Expect a mean above 0.79 with no collapsed seed. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.79.
entries.last_analysis: The observed target is shifted by X/2 in x. Adding a rolled copy of the input (dual-frame) fixes this: dev success went from 0 to 0.59. The learned circular row conv also worked but scored lower (0.35). Cutting PPO epochs from 4 to 2 at 256 envs gave the best result so far (r2c1, 0.79, both seeds close). Most failures look like seeds collapsing to DONE-only. That happened with 1 epoch (0.21/0.00), with gamma 0.99 (0.00/0.32 and 0.00/0.00), and in one seed with 128 envs. The sign is consistent: a longer horizon makes it look worse to keep placing randomly than to stop, and more frequent noisy updates lock in that choice. The two architecture additions (dilated conv, global broadcast) scored lower, partly through fewer samples and partly through seed luck. For the last round, I keep the r2c1 network and recipe and change one thing per trial to make collapse less likely: shorter horizon, more entropy, or near-uniform output initialisation.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on both seeds, and training success was also 0. The trials covered more samples, more exploration, a DONE prior, deeper nets, dense and MLP heads, and flip or transpose heads, so no single idea has shown a signal. One factor has gone unnoticed: every recipe so far cut the number of gradient steps. The default makes 32 updates × 4 epochs × 32 minibatches = 4,096 steps; r1c1 made about 1,900 and r1c3 about 1,660. Getting an exact build depends on precise per-anchor decisions about where each brick lands, which may need many small, low-noise updates rather than more fresh samples. In this final round I test (a) the baseline with about 2× the gradient steps on 64-sample minibatches; (b) a head whose learned convolution has the brick's own footprint as its kernel, so it sees each covered cell individually, plus that recipe; (c) global self-attention so every cell sees the whole design, to help with ordering and with choosing DONE.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I have to choose using priors and the structure of the design space. Every trial trained without errors. Two ideas look like the most promising directions. First, the FootHead, which pairs landing information with each cell, targets the main skill the task needs: judging whether a placement is correct and sealing nothing it shouldn't. Second, recipes with fewer epochs give more fresh designs, and the budget favours that because training designs never repeat. These two ideas have only been combined at 2 epochs (r3c1). The deep dilated trunk with a global summary (r2c2) is the only test of wider context without attention, and it was never paired with the FootHead or the 2-epoch recipe. Because this is the final round and selection uses real 2-seed scores, I propose three strong combinations that differ from each other. Each one adds a single change on top of the FootHead with fewer epochs, which raises the chance that at least one beats the start.

entries.label: r3c3
entries.name: Mirror head, r2c2 recipe, lr 0.002
entries.hypothesis: Same as r2c2, but with the learning rate doubled to 0.002. r2c2's training success first rose only between 25% and 50% of training and was still climbing at the end, so the run is limited by learning speed. Linear decay and gradient clipping should keep the late phase stable. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.946 or either seed becomes unstable (below 0.85).
entries.last_analysis: The left-right flip of trunk features before the footprint pool head is what makes learning work: without it, scores stay at 0, and a learned column mixer (r1c3) failed. The recipe is the next biggest lever. Two PPO epochs with 64 minibatches and gamma 0.97 lifted the score from about 0.74 to about 0.95 (r2c2 0.946, r3c3 0.949; seeds within 0.03 of each other). Two runs that cut gradient steps had a seed collapse (r1c2 and r3c2, one epoch). Doubling lr to 0.002 sped up early learning: training success was 0.17 at 25% of training versus 0.006. Training success was still rising at the end, so learning speed still limits these runs. The global-context head was no better under the good recipe (0.928). The remaining dev failures are few, and the best runs place almost nothing outside the target (0.10 cells per episode), so the last errors are probably about build order or the final brick. With one round left, I'm making safe, single-change recipe refinements of r3c3.

entries.label: r4c2
entries.name: Mirrored head, 1 epoch, 64 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same network as r3c1, with 1 PPO epoch (about 400k samples) and 64 minibatches of 64 samples each. That doubles the gradient steps per update, which offsets the loss of the second epoch while every sample is still seen only once. Fresh data and more optimiser steps should together beat r3c1. Refuted if mean dev success is at or below 0.90, or clearly below the plain 1-epoch candidate.
entries.last_analysis: Every trial without the x-mirrored footprint head collapsed to an immediate DONE and scored 0. With the mirror, the task is learnable. The biggest gain so far came from more samples: dropping from 4 PPO epochs to 2 roughly doubled the samples and moved dev success from 0.65 to 0.90 (seeds 0.94 and 0.86), well beyond the ~0.2 seed spread. A longer credit horizon (0.62), landing-layer attention (0.59), a deeper dilated net (0.35) and the orientation-agnostic head (0.48) all scored at or below the mirrored baseline. r3c1's training success levelled off near 0.87 from 75% of training onward, and its dev IoU is 0.99, so the remaining failures are small ordering or completion errors. For the last round I keep the r3c1 network. I test 1 PPO epoch (about 400k samples), 1 epoch with smaller minibatches (more gradient steps), and a wider trunk at 1 epoch, which keeps about r3c1's sample count and tests whether capacity is the limit.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored 0 on dev and also 0 on training success. That held across recipes (1 to 4 epochs, gamma 0.9 to 0.99, 98k to 405k steps) and across architectures (footprint-pooling head, per-layer logsumexp, conv head with mask inputs, transformer). Seed noise cannot explain this. Even the easy designs with no overhangs, which a greedy 1x1 policy could build, were never built exactly, even with exploration during training. Something structural is wrong. Since the world "may not behave as described", the most likely cause is that action indices do not map to grid cells as the spec states. The axes might be transposed or flipped, the anchor might differ, or DONE might sit at a different index. Every head so far assumed spatial alignment between feature cells and action indices; a 3x3 conv can absorb a one-cell shift but not a transpose. Final round: dense action heads that learn any index-to-cell mapping, including where DONE is.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: I can't see any scores, so I can't rank the trials. All I know is that all 9 trials trained without errors or time-limit kills. So the networks fit the time limit easily, and recipes with more samples are safe: 2 epochs gave about 231k steps (r3c3) with no time problem. Each run has only 2 seeds, so its score will be noisy. Since this is the last round, I'm combining ideas we've already tested rather than trying something untested. I'm pairing the 2-epoch, long-horizon recipe (more fresh samples, which suits a stream of always-new designs) with each of the three main network families: the per-layer token head, the global-context trunk, and the baseline with more gradient steps. That gives three different chances to beat the starting architecture. Every file below makes one clear change from an earlier trial.

entries.label: r4c3
entries.name: Axial + ent0.03 + 90 short updates
entries.hypothesis: Same as r3c2 (entropy 0.03), but each update collects 64 environments × 16 steps and splits them into 16 minibatches of 64 samples. That gives about 90 PPO updates instead of 45, with twice the Adam steps and fresher policies. Earlier, more frequent updates helped (r1c2 over r1c1), and training was still rising at the end. Refuted if dev success is at or below 0.37. A collapse of either seed would mean the shorter rollouts give GAE estimates that are too noisy.
entries.last_analysis: The main barrier was the hidden 4-column shift. Full-span circular axial mixing (rowmix plus colmix) solved it: starting from 0, these runs place about 99% of their cells inside the target. All the gains since then came from the training recipe. Frequent updates (64 environments × 32 steps) helped. Two epochs and the 1x lean network both collapsed toward DONE or weak results. A longer horizon did not help. Two changes each raised the best seed: an entropy coefficient of 0.03 (r3c2, 0.37, the best mean) and 64-sample minibatches (r3c1, 0.457 on one seed). Seed variance is still about ±0.15, so single comparisons are weak. In the traces the agent places correct bricks but stops with DONE before upper layers and some columns are complete, and training success was still rising at the end. More optimiser progress per sample and continued exploration look like the levers. With 3 trials left, I am combining and extending the two changes that helped on the best network.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: r3c2 + 32 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r3c2, but n_minibatches goes from 16 to 32. This doubles the gradient steps per update (128 samples per minibatch) at no counted compute cost, so the number of training samples is unchanged. Learning was still rising at the end, so faster learning from the same data should raise dev success and help the slow seed. Refuted if 2-seed dev success falls below about 0.55.
entries.last_analysis: Lining the shifted target up with the build was the key fix: the X/2 shift-back took dev success from 0 to about 0.6. Passing the per-cell stem features into the footprint head (r3c2) gave the best result, 0.70 (seeds 0.50 and 0.90), but that gain is within seed noise. Seed spread is very large. Moving the recipe away from ppo_epochs 2 with the default gamma did worse: 1 epoch, gamma 0.99 and 2x more updates all scored lower, and a deeper trunk collapsed to instant DONE. Training success was still rising at the end of every good run. In r3c2's trace the agent stops before placing one 1x2 overhang brick that needs exact per-cell landing reasoning, which pooled max/min/mean features lose. Two cheap levers remain: more gradient steps on the same samples (smaller minibatches add no counted compute), and a head that sees each footprint cell's features separately.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored 0 on dev and had 0 training success. That covers the starting net, the layer scorer, the conv+FC hybrid and a plain MLP, each with low-entropy, high-entropy, 1-epoch and slow recipes. Changing the recipe alone did not move the score, and nothing has shown a signal above noise. My best guess is that greedy exact builds need precise per-placement checks that the current heads cannot compute well. To place a brick correctly, the net must find the footprint's landing layer, the maximum column height under the footprint. Then it must check, for every footprint cell, that the target has a cell at that layer and no empty target gap below it. Pooling min, max and mean over the footprint, as the PoolHead does, cannot express this two-stage dependency. In this last round I test a head that does the two stages explicitly: pool learned landing features over the footprint, then judge each footprint cell with a shared MLP and pool the judgements. The three candidates use different recipes and inputs.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials trained cleanly, but scores are hidden, so I can't tell which trunk or recipe is best. In the final round I spread bets across good-looking variants. Structurally, the pooling head looks weakest. It pools max, min and mean separately per channel, so it can't easily match each cell's height with whether the target has a cell at the landing layer (the max height under the footprint). That is needed to judge 'fills only target cells and seals no gaps'. A learned convolution with a kernel the size of the footprint sees every footprint cell's features together and can learn these comparisons. Plan: put this footprint-convolution head on (1) the r2c1 trunk and recipe, (2) the 2-epoch, more-samples recipe of r3c1, and (3) a 4-block trunk with the legal-action mask as input. Varying recipe and depth hedges against seed noise and hidden scores.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: Flip-only, 64 envs
entries.hypothesis: Halve n_envs to 64 with 8 minibatches (128 samples each, as in r3c2). Samples stay the same, but there are about 120 policy updates instead of 60. Doubling the updates raised the mean from 0.64 to 0.89, and the curve was still rising, so doubling again should improve sample use. Refuted if the mean falls below about 0.85 or a seed collapses, which would mean the updates have become too noisy.
entries.last_analysis: Two things clearly mattered. First, the flip: running the network in the agent's own mirrored action frame (flip-only) was needed for any success, while learned axis-mixing failed. Second, more frequent updates: r3c2 has the same samples as r2c1 but twice as many policy updates, and it scored 0.89 with both seeds high (0.88 and 0.91). r2c1 scored 0.64 with seeds 0.84 and 0.43. Every run that lost samples or got noisier did worse: the deeper trunk, the cheap recipe with high entropy, and 3 epochs on the flip-concat network. Small output initialisation and gamma 0.99 gave nothing clear. In r3c2 the learning curve was still rising at the end (0.85 training success). This is the last round, so the safest gains are recipe refinements of r3c2 along the axis that worked: more, smaller updates. One candidate also tests more samples per update through extra epochs. I keep the architecture fixed so that each result is easy to read.

entries.label: r4c1
entries.name: r2c2 with 32 minibatches
entries.hypothesis: Same as r2c2, with 32 minibatches instead of 16 (64 samples each). This doubles the gradient steps per update (about 7.6k in total) while keeping the samples and the 79 updates. r3c1 to r2c2 suggests that more gradient steps help. Refuted if 2-seed dev success is at or below 0.90, or a seed collapses.
entries.last_analysis: Flipping each placement score map in x so it lines up with the action indices was the decisive change. Every trial without it collapsed to choosing DONE (0.0); with it the same start net reached 0.67 under the default recipe. More policy updates then raised this to 0.90 in r2c2, which used 128 envs, 3 epochs and 16 minibatches, giving 79 updates and about 3.8k gradient steps. The variants of r2c2 all did worse. Cutting to 2 epochs and 8 minibatches (r3c1) gave 0.07 with only about 1.8k gradient steps. Adding a global broadcast gave 0.86/0.40. Raising gamma to 0.99 gave 0.95 on one seed and 0.0 on the other. Results vary hugely between seeds, and one failure mode is a seed that never learns. The pattern so far is that more optimiser updates and gradient steps help. When the trained net does work, its failures are rare wrong cells (0.25 extra cells per episode), which points to how precisely the head judges each footprint. This round tests more gradient steps, more updates, and a deeper footprint head.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0, both on dev and on training success. That covers bigger heads, layer-wise heads, attention, the mask as input, layout-agnostic dense heads, a pure MLP, and recipes giving up to about 426k steps. Since even the layout-free MLP never succeeds while sampling during training, an action-layout twist alone probably does not explain it. A likely shared failure is that learning collapses. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they earn negative reward, while DONE returns exactly 0. The policy can learn to stop early and then stop exploring before it can tell which placements are good. Every trial used lr 1e-3, default initialisation and entropy of 0.01 or less. Untested so far: stronger entropy, lower learning rate, normalised trunks, and near-uniform starting policies. With one round left, I put all three candidates on exploration and optimisation rather than layout.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: Scores are hidden, so the analysis rests on how well each design fits the task. In this world a brick's fate depends on where it lands. The per-layer footprint head (r2c1) makes the "does it land at z and match the target" check local to one layer, so it is the strongest guess. All three trials ran without errors, and the 1-epoch run reached 315k steps within the time limit. This is the last round and selection takes the best trial, so I combine plausible gains instead of testing one change at a time. (1) 1 epoch plus whole-episode, longer-horizon rollouts: the most fresh designs, with credit for irreversible mistakes. (2) A shared 3x3 conv within each layer before the footprint pooling, so the head can see same-layer neighbours when choosing how to split a layer into bricks. (3) Column attention with 1 epoch, which recovers the samples lost to the attention block's extra compute.

entries.label: r2c2
entries.name: best + ppo_epochs 2
entries.hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r1c2, but ppo_epochs is 2. That gives about 1.86 times as many environment steps (about 200k) and twice as many updates. This separates the effect of the epoch count from the deeper trunk in r1c3, which changed both. Refuted if dev success falls below about 0.70, which would mean the extra data does not make up for the weaker optimisation of each batch.
entries.last_analysis: The circular (1, X) row-conv stem is the key perceptual fix: it let the network undo the wrapped 4-column target shift and moved dev success from 0 to 0.40. The recipe gave the rest. n_envs 128 with ent_coef 0.02 reached 0.75, and ppo_epochs 2 on top reached 0.877 (r2c2, seeds 0.90 and 0.85). So this setup is limited by data and by the number of updates. Pushing further, with ppo_epochs 1 or n_envs 64 at epochs 2, gave a bimodal result: one seed near 0.88 and one at 0.0, which looks like early collapse. gamma 0.99 gave 0.816, which may be noise but is not better. The deeper trunk and the split stem did not help. In this last round, the 4-seed retrain rewards robustness as well as peak score. I test three single changes to r2c2: zero-initialised output layers, against collapse; a higher learning rate, for faster learning; and a slimmer row stem that brings compute to about 1x, which buys about 20% more samples.

entries.label: r3c1
entries.name: Roll-concat, 3 epochs, 128 envs
entries.hypothesis: Same network as r2c1. The recipe changes to ppo_epochs 3, n_envs 128 and 16 minibatches of 128 samples. That gives about 35% more environment steps (about 158k) and about 77 policy updates instead of 29, with about the same number of gradient steps as r2c1. r2c2's failed seed probably came from its large minibatches and halved gradient steps, which this avoids. Refuted if the 2-seed mean falls below about 0.5 or a seed collapses to DONE.
entries.last_analysis: The target channels are shown rolled by X/2 along x. That explains why every agent without a fix collapsed to DONE in round 1. Concatenating a copy of the observation rolled by X/2 solved this. After that, the recipe mattered most. Going from r2c1 (0.59, 29 updates) to r3c1 (0.89, 77 updates of 2048 samples, 3 epochs, minibatches of 128) shows that more frequent updates help. r3c1's training success was still rising at the end of its budget. Running 2 epochs with 256-sample minibatches risked a collapsed seed (r2c2). Gamma 0.99 hurt (0.41). Row/column context did not help (0.57 vs 0.59). The layer-factored head beat the plain head under the same default recipe (0.75 vs 0.59). That gap is larger than the seed noise we have seen, and that head has not yet been tried with the better recipe. For this final round I am testing: (1) the layer head with r3c1's recipe; (2) r3c1 with twice as many smaller updates; (3) both changes together.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All 9 trials scored exactly 0, on dev and on training success. That covers different heads (pooled, footprint-window, per-layer, dense, attention), different recipes and different horizons. Because the network made no difference, I suspect one cause affects every trial. My best guess is that the policy collapses to calling DONE. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so their reward is negative (about -0.09 per step), while DONE gives 0. The DONE logit gains early, episodes get short, and the agent rarely samples the good placements it needs to learn from. Normalised advantages and an entropy coefficient of 0.01 do little to stop this. I could not observe this directly; it is an inference. The last round tests remedies for this collapse: a high entropy bonus, a longer discount horizon so that future positive placements outweigh stopping, and a DONE logit that learns more slowly. Two use the cheap baseline network and one uses the window head, which had the most detailed per-placement view of the cells.

entries.label: r3c2
entries.name: mirror head, lr 0.002
entries.hypothesis: Same as r1c2 but with the learning rate doubled to 0.002, still decaying linearly to 0. Training success was still rising at the end, so learning seems limited by how fast the policy improves per update, and a larger step should get further on the same 158k samples. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is at or below 0.87, or if a seed becomes unstable or collapses to DONE. That would mean step size is not the bottleneck.
entries.last_analysis: Mirroring the trunk features to match the hidden landing rule is what makes learning work. Without it the agent collapses to DONE. With the default recipe it reaches 0.53, and with more, smaller updates (128 envs, 3 epochs) about 0.88–0.89. Doubling lr to 0.002 gave the best result so far, 0.93, with both seeds at 0.93. The other changes landed within noise of 0.89: longer horizon (0.876), 2 epochs (0.886) and a four-view flip bank (0.90). A 3x3 head projection did worse (0.65) because it is costly and gets fewer samples. Learned remapping (r1c3) and very small batches (r2c1) failed. Dev IoU is about 0.99, so the remaining failures are mostly overhang and ordering errors. One trace has matching column heights but the wrong cells filled. This is the last round, so I will refine the r3c2 recipe, which has the best evidence behind it, with one change per candidate: a higher lr, more samples, or less entropy for sharper greedy policies.

entries.label: r3c2
entries.name: 2 epochs + entropy 0.03
entries.hypothesis: Same as r2c1 (2 PPO epochs, about 231k steps) but ent_coef rises to 0.03. It tests the same anti-collapse fix at an epoch count between the stable 3-epoch r1c2 and the more sample-rich 1-epoch run. Compared with the 1-epoch candidate, it shows which epoch count is best once collapse is controlled. Refuted if a seed collapses to near 0, or if the mean is not above 0.89.
entries.last_analysis: Flipping the head's x-axis is the key fix: placement actions are mirrored in x. Every unflipped network collapsed to choosing DONE at once. Beyond that, the main risk is collapse caused by seed luck. Placements are penalised early in training while DONE scores 0. So 1 epoch (r2c3, r3c1, r3c3) and 2 epochs at entropy 0.01 (r2c1) each lost at least one seed to DONE. Lowering lr made collapse certain. With 2 epochs and entropy 0.03 (r3c2), both seeds survived, giving the best score, 0.936 (0.926/0.945). 3 epochs at entropy 0.01 (r1c2, 0.89) was stable but had fewer samples. The architecture changes so far (both orientations plus depth; stem skip into the head) did worse, partly through slower learning. Dev IoU is about 0.99, so the remaining errors are small. For this final round I make single changes to r3c2: a stronger entropy bonus, 3 epochs with entropy 0.03, and one cheap dilated residual conv for context.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and 0 on training success in the last 10% too, across every seed. Three kinds of change made no difference: recipes (1, 2 or 4 epochs; 74 to 300 updates), heads (footprint pooling, a free conv head, a transposed head, a global MLP head) and per-layer structure. Trials took 30 to 180 s, far below the 900 s limit, so time is not the constraint. Since the networks differ so much and all score 0, I suspect a mismatch in the world rather than slow learning. One candidate is a global spatial misalignment, for example the target shown permuted or shifted relative to the build or the actions. Local convolutions cannot learn that. The flat MLP head could, but it is data-hungry. For this last round I test three ways to mix information globally while keeping weights shared across cells: an MLP-Mixer, a conv network with learned cell-to-cell mixing, and a transformer with learned positions. Any score above 0 would be selected.

entries.label: start
entries.name: starting architecture
entries.last_analysis: No scores are visible, so I can only reason from priors and from which trials ran cleanly. All 9 trials trained without errors. Two ideas recur. On the network side, a per-layer head lines each brick's landing layer up with the missing target cells. Giving it the layers below and above makes support and overhangs local features, which suits a game where bricks drop and order matters. On the recipe side, fewer PPO epochs give more fresh designs under a fixed compute budget. Since 2-seed noise is large, this last round should combine the most plausible ideas instead of testing new ones. I propose: (1) the richest layer head (r3c1) with 1 PPO epoch, giving about 1.6 times its sample count; (2) the starting network with 1 epoch, a clean test of the sample-count idea at about 425k steps; (3) the light layer head (r3c2) plus the adjacent-layer inputs, keeping 1 epoch. Each has one main change from a trial that already ran.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

STEM = 64
COL = 48
WIDTH = 40
PROJ = 32
HID = 32


class PoolHead(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c, footprints, proj, hid):
        super().__init__()
        self.fps = [(int(a), int(b)) for a, b in footprints]
        self.proj = nn.Conv2d(c, proj, 1)
        self.mix = nn.ModuleList([nn.Conv2d(3 * proj, hid, 1) for _ in self.fps])
        self.outs = nn.ModuleList([nn.Conv2d(hid, 1, 1) for _ in self.fps])

    def forward(self, f):
        p = self.proj(f)
        res = []
        for (dy, dx), mix, out in zip(self.fps, self.mix, self.outs):
            if dy * dx == 1:
                mx, mn, av = p, p, p
            else:
                q = F.pad(p, (0, dx - 1, 0, dy - 1))
                mx = F.max_pool2d(q, (dy, dx), stride=1)
                mn = -F.max_pool2d(-q, (dy, dx), stride=1)
                av = F.avg_pool2d(q, (dy, dx), stride=1)
            h = F.relu(mix(torch.cat([mx, mn, av], dim=1)))
            res.append(out(h))
        return torch.cat(res, dim=1).flatten(1)


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(spec.in_channels, STEM, 1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(STEM, COL, 1), nn.ReLU())
        self.c1 = nn.Conv2d(COL, WIDTH, 3, padding=1)
        self.c2 = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, WIDTH, 3, padding=1)
        self.head = PoolHead(WIDTH, spec.footprints, PROJ, HID)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, 64), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(64, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(64, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        s = self.stem(obs)
        x = F.relu(self.c1(s))
        f = F.relu(x + self.c2(x))
        place = self.head(f)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)
